Converted executor.lua's four ledger-touching methods to callbacks after establishing the synchronous contract could not back a real subprocess ledger without violating AGENTS.md section 10; recorded that contract change on louiselm-qbr.3.6. Tests: tests/workflow/ledger_spec.lua (7 new, argv/env contract, back-edge composition, replay, failure surfaces); executor_spec.lua rewritten to an async double and grown 6 to 12 cases covering the scheduling boundary, the in-flight guard, disposal during an in-flight call, and a refused reservation leaving no Generator; tests/workflow/ledger_integration_spec.lua drives the real louiselm-capture binary and proves AC1 jointly — an Agent br create and an executor back-edge exhaust one shared ceiling of two — plus AC2 reserve/confirm/release end to end. Both new invariants verified by mutation (guard disabled, and the br create replaced with /bin/true). Gates: MiniTest 0 fails, LuaLS 0 problems, StyLua, API appendix, cargo test/clippy/fmt all clean.

comments.author: claude/004cc6f2-daa2-4bdf-b0b1-136c23318dc6
comments.text:
Design record for the adapter.

Back-edge identity: confirm_generated_work requires a non-empty external id, and a back-edge traversal produces no Beads issue to name. The traversal's own mutation id is used as the external id, so the recorded output row reads kind=back_edge, external_id=<mutation id>. It is unique per traversal, never empty, and replaying it hits the store's existing generated_issue(mutation_id) == Some(issue_id) short circuit instead of double-charging. consume is therefore reserve(1) followed by confirm, with a reserve reply of 'consumed' short-circuiting as an already-completed replay.

In-flight guard: the executor now refuses a second mutating operation while a ledger call is outstanding. Without it two concurrent advance() calls both pass validation and both charge, spending two units for one logical move — the async rewrite created that window, so it is closed in the same change. Covered by 'refuses a second operation while a ledger call is in flight', verified to fail when the guard is disabled.

Disposal ordering: dispose() sets status before attempting the release, so a ledger that is already unreachable cannot hold a workflow open. A failed release is reported and the capacity is left to the service-side reaper, which is the component that owns reclaiming a reservation nobody is returning for. Late ledger replies after disposal are ignored rather than allowed to revive state.

Lesson routed to AGENTS.md section 8: a seam that will be backed by I/O takes an async signature from the start, because a synchronous double freezes a synchronous contract into the interface. That is the general form of this slice's cost.

title: Give the mock Agent work generation and author a looping qa-review fixture
description:
## Goal

Supply the two test doubles `louiselm-qbr.3.2.6.5` AC4 needs and that do not exist today: a mock Agent that can actually generate work, and a qa-review workflow fixture that actually loops.

## Why both are missing

- `lua/louiselm/dev/mock_agent.lua` has modes `echo|static|permission|crash` and **no notion of generating work**. It cannot be told to invoke `br create`, and has no hook to shell out through `scripts/run-tools/br`. Without this, a mock-Agent-driven Run cannot consume budget at all, so AC4 has nothing to bound.
- **No workflow fixture pairs a Generator with an automatic back-edge.** `tests/workflow/validate_spec.lua`'s `reference_manifest()` puts `generates` on the **route** stage, not qa-review, and qa-review's back-edge is `resolver = "human"`, which `executor.lua` deliberately never charges. `executor_spec.lua`'s `loop_manifest()` has the automatic bounded back-edge but no Generator.

AC4 needs *one stage that both generates work and loops automatically* — that combination is authored nowhere.

## Correction to this issue's original scope

This issue originally directed the fixture to be authored as real `SKILL.md` documents fed through the existing discovery path. **That path does not exist.** `skills/metadata.lua` reads only `name`, `description`, `metadata.short-description`, `disable-model-invocation`, and `phase`; every workflow stage key appears nowhere outside `lua/louiselm/workflow/`, and every manifest in the repository is a hand-built table in a spec. `louiselm-qbr.8` settling that workflows are discovered documents is a decision about what to build, not a description of what runs.

Filed as `louiselm-qbr.3.7` under `qbr.3` rather than absorbed here, because building the parser is the next piece of the deferred execution engine and folding it into a test-double slice is the scope reallocation the 2026-08-27 pause refused to make. It does not block the parent's acceptance: AC4 claims budget enforcement, and a manifest bounds a loop identically whether parsed from YAML or written as a table.

## Scope

- In scope: a mock Agent capability that performs a bounded, deterministic sequence of work-generating invocations through the Run's `br` shim; a shared qa-review manifest fixture whose single stage carries both `generates` and an automatic bounded back-edge.
- Out of scope: the end-to-end assertions themselves (sibling slice), workflow document parsing (`louiselm-qbr.3.7`), any real Agent behaviour.

## Design constraint

Per AGENTS.md section 5, the mock is a test double and not a protocol specification; if it accepts what a real Agent would reject, that permissiveness is a defect. Generation reaches the broker by name so the Run environment's `PATH` decides which `br` answers, exactly as it does for a real Agent.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The mock Agent can be configured to attempt a bounded, deterministic number of `br create` invocations through the Run shim, with no network, credentials, or real agent binary.
- Generation stops at the first refusal and reports the reason, so an exhausted budget is distinguishable from a broken broker.
- The qa-review fixture passes `Workflow.validate` and yields a stage with both an automatic bounded back-edge and a `generates` block, with every bound the budget proof depends on narrowable by the caller.

## Not covered

The Park/ceiling/cycle assertions that consume these doubles.
close_reason: Added generate_count/generate_title to lua/louiselm/dev/mock_agent.lua: the mock now attempts a bounded number of br create invocations through the Run's shim on PATH, stops at the first refusal, and replies with a JSON summary of what was created and what refused it so a budget Park is distinguishable from a broken broker. The option composes with any existing mode rather than being a new mode, since generating work is orthogonal to how the Agent answers. Added lua/louiselm/dev/reference_workflow.lua supplying the qa-review manifest whose single stage carries both a Generator and an automatic bounded back-edge — the combination that turns a bounded graph into an unbounded effect, and which is authored nowhere else in the repository. Tests: tests/mock/agent_spec.lua gains 'generates bounded work through the Run br shim' and 'stops generating at the first refusal and reports it' (7 to 9 cases, driven against a fake br on PATH with an invocation counter); tests/workflow/reference_workflow_spec.lua guards the fixture's defining property so a future edit cannot silently make the sibling budget proof vacuous. Lesson routing: the discovery-to-manifest gap this slice uncovered is filed as louiselm-qbr.3.7 and the correction recorded in this issue's description and comments; no AGENTS.md rule warranted. Gates: MiniTest 0 fails, LuaLS 0 problems, StyLua, API appendix clean.

title: Prove the bounded qa-review loop Parks at its ceiling with clean cycles
description:
## Goal

The motivating scenario of the whole `louiselm-qbr.3.2` line, proven end to end: a qa-review workflow that repeatedly produces Beads issues runs up to its Run ceiling, then **Parks** — with exactly that many issues created, no mutation beyond the bound, and `br dep cycles` empty throughout, demonstrating that the *budget* stopped growth rather than cycle detection.

This is `louiselm-qbr.3.2.6.5` AC4 and AC5. It is the acceptance the parent exists for.

## Why it is not proven today

No test in the repository crosses the Lua/capture-service boundary for budget accounting. The highest-water-mark integration is `capture-service/tests/cli.rs:222`, which spawns the real binary but drives it with a fake `br` shell script against a `BEADS_DB` path that is never an actual Beads workspace, and never involves Lua or the executor. And `br dep cycles` appears nowhere in the repository outside `AGENTS.md:63` prose — no test invokes it, and no test ever creates a real Beads workspace to invoke it against.

## Scope

- In scope: a deterministic end-to-end test driving the qa-review fixture through the executor and the real ledger against a **temporary real Beads workspace**, plus the restart/pending-reservation and cancellation assertions the parent's Testing section names.
- Out of scope: the CLI surface, ledger adapter, mock Agent mode, and fixture — all blocking sibling slices this consumes.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The loop produces issues up to the declared ceiling and then Parks, with the created-issue count **exactly** equal to the ceiling — not at-most, not at-least.
- No Beads mutation occurs after the Park.
- `br dep cycles` returns empty at every checkpoint, so the stop is attributable to the budget and not to cycle detection.
- A restart with a pending reservation reconciles rather than double-charging or stranding capacity (`runs.rs:548` `pending_generation_ids` is the reconciliation hook).
- Cancellation mid-loop releases the outstanding reservation.
- Deterministic: no network, no credentials, no real agent binary; a real Beads workspace created and torn down by the test.

## Not covered

The AC6 residuals (per-Run isolation, Provenance actor resolution, resume envelope non-widening), which are a sibling slice.
close_reason: Added tests/workflow/budget_acceptance_spec.lua, the first test in the repository to cross Lua, capture-service, and a real Beads workspace for budget accounting. Drives the reference qa-review loop through the real executor and ledger against a br-init'd throwaway workspace: two rounds of file-a-finding plus take-the-back-edge exhaust a ceiling of four, the third create is refused, exactly two issues exist, no further mutation occurs after the Park, the executor Parks rather than erroring, and br dep cycles is empty at every checkpoint so the budget rather than cycle detection is provably what stopped growth. Also covers disposal releasing an outstanding reservation and a restart recognizing a pending reservation instead of double-spending it. Verified discriminating by mutation: widening the ceiling to six fails the refusal assertion. Gates: MiniTest 0 fails across the full suite, LuaLS 0 problems, StyLua, API appendix clean. Skips with an explicit message when louiselm-capture or br is unavailable rather than silently passing.

comments.author: claude/004cc6f2-daa2-4bdf-b0b1-136c23318dc6
comments.text:
Scenario shape, recorded because the arithmetic is what makes the assertion exact rather than approximate. Ceiling 4 buys exactly two rounds: each round files one finding through the shim (1 beads_issue unit) and takes the automatic back-edge for another round (1 back_edge unit). The third round's create is refused, so exactly 2 issues exist. Asserting equality rather than an upper bound matters — at-most passes trivially if generation silently stops early, and at-least passes if the bound leaks.

br dep cycles is asserted empty at every round boundary and after the Park. That is the load-bearing part of AC5: without it, a halting loop proves nothing about the budget, because cycle detection could have been what stopped it. The workflow is acyclic by construction and still unbounded, which is the whole reason this budget exists.

Discrimination checked by mutation rather than trusted: widening the ceiling from 4 to 6 fails the test at the refusal assertion, so the halt is genuinely attributable to the ceiling and not to an incidental error.

Restart case: replaying the same mutation identity against a durable Run with 2 of 2 units already reserved returns 'pending' rather than reserving a second 2 units. If idempotency were broken the reply would be 'exhausted' instead, so the assertion distinguishes the two failure modes rather than merely observing that something was refused.

title: Prove Run isolation, generated-issue Provenance, and resume envelope limits
description:
## Goal

Close the three residual sub-claims of `louiselm-qbr.3.2.6.5` AC6, each of which is currently structurally plausible but untested.

## The three gaps

1. **Concurrent Runs do not pool capacity.** `capture-service/tests/generation.rs:260` (`concurrent_generators_cannot_overspend_one_run`) proves two mutations *inside one Run* cannot overspend. It does not prove *two distinct Runs* stay isolated. Per-Run isolation is structurally obvious — one record per Run id — but obvious is not proven, and pooling would be a silent budget escape.
2. **Provenance resolves every generated issue to its Session actor.** `runs.rs:540` `generation_actor` stamps the attached `session_id` at creation, and `tests/provenance/correlate_spec.lua:88` classifies actor edges independently — but nothing joins a *generated* issue back through `louiselm.provenance.correlate` to the Session that generated it. The two halves are tested in isolation and never meet.
3. **Resume cannot widen another envelope axis.** `runs.rs:677` `raise_generated_work_ceiling` structurally touches only `generated_work.ceiling`, and `runs.rs:434` asserts revisioned idempotency — but no test asserts that a resume attempting to widen a *different* axis is refused. Per the Park vocabulary record (`louiselm-k1fv`): "Resuming a Park is an operator act, never an Agent act, and cannot exceed the original envelope on any axis." That is a stated invariant with no test behind it.

## Scope

- In scope: the three regressions above.
- Out of scope: new enforcement code, unless a test proves an invariant is actually violated — in which case file the defect as its own bug per AGENTS.md before fixing.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Two Runs with independent ceilings each exhaust their own budget without either consuming the other's capacity, and exhaustion of one does not Park the other.
- An issue created through `run generate` resolves through Provenance to the Session actor recorded at generation time, joining the two halves that are currently tested apart.
- A resume that attempts to widen an envelope axis other than the generated-work ceiling is refused, and the refusal is attributable.

## Notes

If any of these turns out to fail rather than pass, that is a finding: file it as a bug with the failing evidence **before** repairing it, per AGENTS.md.
close_reason: All three AC6 residuals now covered, all passing, none revealing a defect. capture-service/tests/runs.rs gains concurrent_runs_do_not_pool_generated_work_capacity (exhausting and Parking one Run leaves a second Run's own unit spendable, so exhaustion is not contagious and capacity is not shared) and raising_a_ceiling_widens_that_axis_and_no_other (park expiry, consumption, reservation, and Session identity are invariant across an operator raise and the following resume, and restating or narrowing the ceiling is refused). tests/workflow/run_provenance_spec.lua joins the two previously separate halves: an issue created through the Run shim against a real Beads workspace is read back out of Beads and resolved through louiselm.provenance.correlate to the Run's attached Session. Gates: cargo test 17/17 in runs, full MiniTest 0 fails, LuaLS 0 problems, StyLua, API appendix, clippy, fmt clean.

comments.author: claude/004cc6f2-daa2-4bdf-b0b1-136c23318dc6
comments.text:
All three residuals passed as written; none exposed a defect, so no bug was filed.

Envelope axes, enumerated because the AC6 claim ('resume cannot widen another envelope axis') is only meaningful once the axes are named. A Run's envelope is generated_work.ceiling, park_ttl_ms, and the attached Session identity. raise_generated_work_ceiling is the single operator widening path: it requires a Parked state, a matching revision, and a strictly greater ceiling. The test now asserts the other axes are invariant across both the raise and the subsequent resume, and that restating or narrowing the ceiling is refused — so 'raise' cannot be repurposed to take capacity away either.

The 'never an Agent act' half of the Park vocabulary claim (louiselm-k1fv) was already covered by run_socket.rs's operator_mutations_require_the_private_capability_and_current_revision; this slice covers the 'cannot exceed the original envelope on any axis' half.

Provenance join: the two halves existed and never met. The broker stamps the attached Run's session_id as the Beads actor and Correlate classifies actor strings, but nothing proved an issue a Run actually created traces back to it. The new spec creates work through the shim against a real Beads workspace, reads the issue back out of Beads rather than trusting the create reply, and resolves created_by through Correlate to the Run's Session.

title: Hold durable Run state and reap expired Parks in capture-service
description:
## Problem Statement

A Park waits for human attention, and that wait is measured in hours or days. Neovim's lifetime is
not. Agents are `vim.system` children (`lua/louiselm/acp/transport.lua:164`), so closing the editor
takes the Run's Sessions with it — and, worse, takes the expiry timer too. A Parked Run whose
expiry never fires leaves `br` issues claimed by a Session nobody is running, and `br` has no lease
or heartbeat to reap them. A bound whose enforcer the user can close is not a bound.

## Solution

capture-service holds the durable Run record and reaps expired Parks. Ambitious and narrow: narrow
is the scope, not the effort. The service owns exactly two things — the Run record and the expiry
reaper — and its reaper correctness is load-bearing, not a cron afterthought.

The service does not orchestrate, does not spawn Agents, and does not decide transitions. Neovim
remains the cockpit and drives everything interactive. The service is the only component that can
outlive the editor and reap what the editor abandoned.

Park has two tiers, and admission tells the operator which one they are getting:

- **Warm Park** — same editor lifetime. Turns Cancelled, Sessions alive, resume is exact.
- **Cold Park** — survived an editor exit. Sessions gone; resume is lossy reconstruction via ACP
  `loadSession`, gated on `agentCapabilities.loadSession` (`lua/louiselm/acp/init.lua:252`). An
  Agent without that capability cannot be cold-Parked at all.

## User Stories

1. As an operator, I want a Parked Run to survive closing Neovim, so an unattended run is not
   destroyed by ordinary editor hygiene.
2. As an operator, I want an expired Park reaped even while Neovim is closed, so claimed issues are
   released instead of stranded.
3. As an operator, I want to know at admission whether this Run can be cold-Parked, so I am not
   told tomorrow that yesterday's Park evaporated.
4. As a maintainer reading the backlog, I want a reaped claim release attributable to the Session
   that made the claim, not to a daemon that never held it.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Given a Run record written by Neovim, when Neovim exits, then the record survives and the Run is
   marked cold-Parked.
2. Given a cold-Parked Run whose expiry passes while Neovim is closed, when the reaper runs, then
   claims are released, Sessions are Disposed, and the Forensics record is retained.
3. Given a Run whose Agent does not advertise `loadSession`, when admission runs, then the operator
   is told cold Park is unavailable for this Run before it starts.
4. Given a reaped Park, when the claim release is inspected through Provenance, then the actor
   resolves to the expired Run's Session identity, not to the service.
5. Given a warm-Parked Run resumed in the same editor lifetime, then resume is exact — no
   `session/load` replay occurs.
6. Given a cold-Parked Run resumed, then the resume is reported as recoverable and lossy, not as
   restored.
7. Given an operator resuming a Park with raised budget, then no other envelope axis is widened.
   Resume is refused if requested by an Agent rather than an operator.
8. The reaper is idempotent and safe across service restarts and concurrent editor sessions.

## Implementation Notes

- The service is Rust under systemd user units, already installed and observed
  (`louiselm-qbr.1.8`), which is exactly why it is the right home: it is the only component with
  a lifetime longer than the editor.
- Rejected alternative: Runs as beads issues. It makes Beads a core dependency, which
  `louiselm-qbr` explicitly refuses; it pollutes `br ready` and `br scheduler` with execution state
  that is not work-to-do; and `br` has no lease concept to express a Park that must expire.
- Rejected alternative: Run state in Neovim persisted across restart. It fails the expiry test
  above — while the editor is closed, nothing reaps.
- Open mechanic to settle in design: the reaper acts as the expired Run's identity so Provenance
  (`louiselm-tsxh`) resolves the release back to the claiming Session. This is a second component
  mutating `br`, so the `--actor` discipline in `AGENTS.md:30` needs an explicit answer for a
  non-interactive actor.
- Accepting this decision is what makes unattended workflow runs possible at all; declining it
  would mean cold Park does not exist and `louiselm-qbr.5.1`'s premise has nothing to stand on.

## Testing Notes

- Reaper behaviour must be tested with the editor genuinely absent, not simulated by a flag —
  the whole point of the decision is what happens when Neovim is not running.
- Cold Park resume needs a mock agent both with and without `loadSession` advertised
  (`lua/louiselm/dev/mock_agent.lua` already advertises it, so the negative case needs a variant).
- Claim-release attribution is verifiable through `br` actor fields; assert on the actor string.
- Physical dogfood: Park a Run, quit Neovim, wait past expiry, confirm `br` claims released.

## Out of Scope

- Validation, admission and the Generator bounds — see the workflow-safety-contracts feature.
- Any orchestration, transition decisions, or Agent spawning inside the service.
- Assessment.
close_reason: Implemented durable cold-Park persistence, operator resume, expiry reaping, and Provenance attribution

comments.author: claude/0929f4e1-c8f2-4717-998f-1902618ce5f8
comments.text:
Decision on the open --actor mechanic, taken 2026-08-26 with maintainer delegation.

Use a composite actor of the form reaper/<expired-run-session-id>, not the bare Session id.

The earlier proposal in the description -- have the reaper act AS the expired Run's Session identity -- is wrong on inspection. AGENTS.md:30 requires the actor point at a transcript someone can actually open, and a bare Session id satisfies that, but it also asserts the Session performed the mutation. Someone opening that transcript to understand a claim release would find no such command in it. That is a different lie from an unattributable daemon, not an improvement on it.

The composite form keeps both properties: the session id is still there to open, and the reaper/ prefix is honest that a non-interactive component acted on that Run's behalf. It is also greppable, so 'what did the reaper release' is answerable.

Open sub-question for implementation: whether Provenance (louiselm-tsxh) parses the prefix or treats the whole string as opaque. Prefer parsing, so a reaped release still correlates to the Session in provenance views rather than appearing as a distinct actor.

comments.author: claude/0929f4e1-c8f2-4717-998f-1902618ce5f8
comments.text: Deferred to match louiselm-qbr.3's posture until louiselm-qbr.3.2.2 lands. It blocks only qbr.3.2.6, which is blocked on .3.2.2 anyway, so leaving it in br ready adds noise without adding a grab.

comments.text: Implementation boundary audit found that capture-service has no Beads or ACP adapter, while this feature's expiry acceptance requires a truthful reaper-originated claim release and Session disposal. Created louiselm-qbr.3.5 to settle the owner and authorized command/outbox boundary; deferring this feature until that decision prevents an unaudited br subprocess or a fake reaper.

comments.text: First durable qbr.3.3 slice implemented in capture-service: RunStore persists cold-Parked Run records as atomic JSON, retains them after disposal, and journals each pre-authorized claim release. reap_expired emits reaper/<session-id> actions through a narrow adapter callback; failed callbacks leave the action pending, while completed actions are not repeated. Tests passed: cargo test --test runs (2), cargo test (all 25), cargo clippy -- -D warnings, cargo fmt, and git diff --check. Remaining: service-loop scheduling, the constrained br adapter/workspace allowlist, and Neovim admission/Park/resume integration. Lesson routing: this issue comment; no AGENTS.md change is warranted.

comments.author: codex/01a03ec2-dede-7c62-958c-0dd56e12b1ee
comments.text:
Async decision, confirmed by maintainer after reviewing Neovim's libuv model (2026-08-26).

Keep pure workflow logic synchronous. At external I/O boundaries, use Neovim-native asynchronous callbacks: vim.system(..., callback) for the local service command and vim.schedule() before any editor/state work. Do not call SystemObj:wait(), block the main loop, or add a coroutine/promise/nvim-nio framework for this one linear request/response bridge.

The service callback is an implementation boundary, not user-facing callback hell: Run transitions only after the durable command result succeeds; failure leaves the Run active and returns a structured error through the existing event/UI boundary. Coroutines are not required for I/O concurrency and do not make CPU-heavy Lua parallel. Reconsider a workflow-local structured task abstraction only when there is a demonstrated multi-step lifecycle (streaming process + RPC + user selection + cancellation/disposal) that callback composition makes materially unclear.

comments.text: Implemented the cold-Park admission metadata slice: Run records now persist configured Agent, ACP Session id, working directory, and the confirmed session/load capability; the Rust store and Lua service boundary reject non-reloadable cold Parks. Added persistence and negative-capability coverage. Verification: full Lua suite 620 cases passed, focused workflow tests passed, cargo test --all-targets passed, cargo clippy --all-targets -D warnings passed, StyLua passed. comments.text: Production admission slice added: Run:park_cold derives the durable record from its single owned live ACP Session, requires initialized Agent/ACP identity, working directory, and advertised loadSession capability, and refuses ambiguous multi-Session Runs. Focused workflow coverage passes (13 cases); full Lua suite passes (623 cases). Remaining: wire a UI/operator entrypoint and cold resume selection, plus Provenance parsing for reaper actors.

comments.text: Added pure Provenance.resolve_actor for Beads actors: reaper/<agent>/<acp-session> resolves to the underlying Session while retaining raw actor and reaper kind; ordinary agent/session actors remain distinguishable; malformed reaper identities are rejected. Added regression coverage. Full Lua suite: 627 cases passed; focused provenance, StyLua, LuaLS, and git diff checks pass. Parent remains open for physical cold-Park dogfood and any remaining service acceptance.

comments.text: Completion evidence (2026-08-26): capture-service now persists reloadable cold-Park metadata, filters expired records from resume discovery, retries claim release through reaper/<session-id>, and retains disposed records. The systemd source unit and environment example configure the Beads workspace and writable .beads boundary; the live user service was rebuilt/restarted and is active with LOUISELM_BEADS_WORKSPACE=/home/lotso/code/louiselm. title: Assess workflow documents for unbounded effects without gating them
description:
## Problem Statement

Validation reads frontmatter only, and that is deliberately narrow: it is pure, binary and free of
any model. But a workflow can be structurally impeccable and still obviously reckless to anyone who
reads it. Nothing in the structural contract notices that.

The maintainer's framing: someone should be able to hand the whole document to a model good at this
and ask whether the workflow is going to burst into flames by unbounding effects.

## Solution

Assessment: a model reads the entire workflow document, prose included, and returns an opinion on
unbounded effects. It has no authority. It never gates execution, never rejects, and never appears
in the same channel as Validation.

Assessment is delivered to an operator at envelope-approval time, alongside `louiselm-qbr.5.1`'s
capability diff — the moment a human is already reading and deciding. That is what keeps it from
being a smuggled warn tier: its output never appears when nobody is there to weigh it.

Verdicts are stored, keyed on `hash(document) + model id + prompt version`. Staleness is expressed
as absence — "no current Assessment" — never as a stale verdict shown as fresh.

## User Stories

1. As an operator approving an unattended run, I want a model's read of the whole document, so
   recklessness that no structural rule catches still reaches me.
2. As an operator, I want Assessment's output next to the capability diff I am already reviewing,
   not in a log I will never open.
3. As a maintainer, I want to find out whether Assessment is any good, by comparing its verdicts
   against what Runs actually did.
4. As a maintainer, I want a second opinion from a different model to be a deliberate act with both
   verdicts on file, rather than nondeterminism I hope does not bite.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Assessment runs in an isolated Session with an empty capability envelope: no tools, no skill
   invocation, no `br` mutation, no filesystem, no network.
2. Given a workflow document containing text instructing the reader to report no hazards, when
   Assessment runs, then nothing in the system acts on that instruction — verified by the envelope,
   not by prompt wording.
3. Assessment never blocks a Run. There is no configuration in which an Assessment verdict prevents
   execution.
4. Assessment output is presented at envelope-approval time and is absent from non-interactive
   paths where no operator is present.
5. Given an unchanged document, model id and prompt version, then the stored verdict is returned
   without a new model call.
6. Given a changed document, then the interface reports "no current Assessment" rather than showing
   the previous verdict.
7. A stored verdict records model id and timestamp, and the operator can request a fresh Assessment
   deliberately, retaining both.
8. Assessment verdicts can be joined against Run outcomes (Parked on budget / escaped / Disposed on
   expiry / completed clean) to produce a calibration report.

## Implementation Notes

- Assessment and Validation are different in kind and must not share a name, an output channel, or
  a call site. Validation may reject; Assessment may only inform.
- The naming avoids "review" (`qa-review`) and "audit" (`br audit`), both taken.
- The reason Assessment is safe is precisely its lack of authority: a workflow document is
  semi-trusted input, and an advisory opinion read by a human has bounded blast radius where a gate
  reading the same text does not. Any future proposal to let Assessment gate should be read as
  removing the property that makes it safe.
- Storage is Provenance-shaped (`louiselm-tsxh`) and should compose with whatever `louiselm-3x9p`
  settles about session-level usage events rather than inventing a parallel store.
- Cost matters: unattended runs fire repeatedly against unchanged documents, so recomputation would
  mean a model call per admission instead of one per document version.

## Testing Notes

- The injection case is the important test and it asserts on capability, not on model output: with
  an empty envelope, a document instructing tool use must produce no tool call.
- Cache-key behaviour is deterministic and testable without a live model by stubbing the verdict.
- Calibration reporting needs Run outcome data, so it depends on the durable Run record.

## Out of Scope

- Any gating, blocking, or rejection behaviour.
- Structural checks of any kind — those belong to Validation.
- Building the capability-envelope review UI itself (`louiselm-qbr.5.1`).

title: Grill-me needed: how does the expiry reaper release Beads claims?
description:
Do not resolve this in passing; it needs an explicit maintainer decision.

Question: how may the capture-service expiry reaper cause Beads claim release and Session disposal while preserving truthful provenance, without turning the capture daemon into a workflow orchestrator or shelling out to an unaudited br process?

Context: louiselm-qbr.3.3 requires cold-Parked Runs to survive Neovim exit and, on expiry, release claims, dispose Sessions, retain forensics, and attribute the release as reaper/<expired-run-session-id>. The existing Rust capture-service owns only local speech-capture files, pairing, and transcription. It has no Beads client, no ACP client, and no workflow command/API boundary. Adding a direct br subprocess would make a service restart perform external work outside the existing approval/audit model; a generic durable record alone cannot satisfy the claim-release acceptance criterion.

Threads to pull:
- Should a dedicated workflow supervisor (rather than capture-service) own the durable Run/reaper lifecycle?
- If capture-service remains the owner, what narrow authenticated command/protocol boundary lets it request releases/disposal?
- How should reaper/<session> be represented so Beads/Provenance can correlate it to the expired Session without claiming the Session ran the command?
- Is a reaper action log/outbox sufficient, and which component is authorized to consume it exactly once?
close_reason: Resolved: durable service owns a journaled cleanup outbox and constrained Beads adapter

comments.text: Maintainer confirmed the durable-service boundary on 2026-08-26: Rust is LouiseLM's durable local service; Neovim remains the interactive cockpit. The service owns durable Run/Park state, expiry, and an append-only cleanup outbox. Its Beads adapter may execute only pre-recorded claim releases, as reaper/<expired-session-id>; it cannot choose work, create issues, invoke skills, spawn Sessions, or decide Run transitions. Each action is journaled before and after execution for restart-safe idempotency. The service exposes one normalized state model with human-facing summaries and machine-readable AX; Android attention delivery is a separate feature. This resolves the question.

comments.text:
Contract change to this issue's delivered API, decided in louiselm-qbr.3.2.6.5.2 with maintainer confirmation on 2026-08-30. The ExecutorLedger contract shipped here is synchronous-return: advance() calls ledger.consume() and reads its verdict inline (executor.lua:180), and begin_generator/record_generator_output/end_generator do the same for reserve/confirm/release. That signature cannot be implemented against the real ledger, which is a louiselm-capture subprocess: the only synchronous way to reach it is vim.system():wait(), and AGENTS.md section 10 forbids blocking the main loop. The contract was shaped by a fake ledger that answers instantly, and this slice's completion note correctly flagged that async service wiring remained the caller's responsibility — this is that responsibility coming due.

Rejected alternatives, recorded so they are not re-proposed: a local budget mirror answering synchronously and reconciling in the background can answer consumed where the real ledger says exhausted, which is the precise budget escape louiselm-qbr.3.2 exists to prevent; and reserving max-iterations up front for back-edges would preserve the synchronous contract but contradicts qbr.3.2.6.5 AC1 (one traversal consumes one unit) and would let a max-iterations 5 loop occupy a ceiling-5 Run immediately. The pay-as-you-go back-edge versus reserve-maximum skill Generator split is deliberate.

Chosen: the four ledger-touching methods become callback-based. Blast radius at decision time was executor.lua plus tests/workflow/executor_spec.lua only — new_executor had zero production callers, just the export at init.lua:60 — so the change is cheapest now and grows with every future caller.

title: Workflow documents cannot become stage manifests: no frontmatter path exists
description:
## Observed

Found on 2026-08-30 while scoping `louiselm-qbr.3.2.6.5.3`, which had been written on the assumption that a workflow fixture could be authored as real `SKILL.md` documents and fed through the existing discovery path.

There is no such path. The workflow validator and executor consume a stage manifest — a table keyed by stage name whose blocks carry `workflow`, `entry`, `outcomes`, `generates`, `back-edge`, `max-iterations`, `on-exhausted`, `generated-work`, and `park-expiry` — and **nothing in the codebase constructs one from a document**.

Evidence:

- `lua/louiselm/skills/metadata.lua:132` (`M.skill`) is the only SKILL.md frontmatter parser. It extracts exactly `name`, `description`, `metadata.short-description`, `disable-model-invocation`, and `phase`. Grepping it for any workflow stage key returns zero hits.
- Every workflow stage key (`outcomes`, `generates`, `back-edge`, `max-iterations`, `on-exhausted`, `generated-work`, `park-expiry`) appears nowhere in the non-test Lua tree outside `lua/louiselm/workflow/` itself.
- Every manifest that exists is a hand-built Lua table inside a spec: `tests/workflow/{executor,validate,cache,run}_spec.lua`.

## Why this matters

`louiselm-qbr.8` settled that workflows persist as graphs of discovered `SKILL.md` documents whose frontmatter declares named outcomes and transitions. `lua/louiselm/workflow/validate.lua` implements the full structural contract for that shape — bounded back-edges, Generator maxima, exhaustion-outcome reachability — and it is thorough. But it validates a shape that only tests ever produce.

The practical consequence is the same class of gap `louiselm-qbr.3.6` closed for stage execution and `louiselm-qbr.3.2.6.5.2` closed for the ledger: a fully specified contract with no production path reaching it. A workflow author cannot today write a workflow document at all.

## Deliberately not folded into the slice that found it

`louiselm-qbr.3.2.6.5.3` was rescoped to a hand-built looping manifest rather than absorbing this work. Building the document-to-manifest parser is the next piece of `louiselm-qbr.3`'s execution engine, which remains deferred, and quietly building it inside a mock-Agent test-double slice is exactly the scope reallocation that the 2026-08-27 pause on `louiselm-qbr.3.2.6.5` correctly refused to make.

This is also not a blocker for `louiselm-qbr.3.2.6.5`'s acceptance. AC4 is a claim about budget enforcement — that a generating loop Parks at its ceiling having created exactly that many issues. A manifest bounds the loop identically whether it was parsed from YAML or written as a table, so the budget contract is provable without this. What is not provable without it is that a *workflow author's document* produces the manifest the budget then bounds.

## Fix direction

Parse the workflow stage block out of SKILL.md frontmatter and assemble the per-workflow manifest that `Workflow.validate` and `Workflow.new_executor` already accept. Reuse `skills/discovery.lua`'s traversal and `lyaml` rather than adding a second frontmatter reader. Keep it structural and total, matching the Validation vocabulary record (`louiselm-p5h0`): parsing decides shape, never prose.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A discovered `SKILL.md` declaring workflow stage frontmatter yields a manifest block that `Workflow.validate` accepts, without any hand-built table.
- A document set spanning several files assembles into one manifest keyed by stage name, and stages belonging to other workflows are excluded.
- Malformed or contradictory stage frontmatter is rejected with an actionable diagnostic rather than silently dropped, and a document with no workflow frontmatter is simply not a stage.
- The existing hand-built manifests in specs can be replaced by parsed fixtures for at least one end-to-end case.

## Not covered

Executing the parsed workflow (owned by `louiselm-qbr.3.6`), Assessment of document prose, and the remainder of `louiselm-qbr.3`.
close_reason: Parse workflow stage frontmatter into validated manifests

comments.author: assistant
comments.text:
**Candidate requirement for this issue's design — not a settled decision.**

When a workflow engine sequences beads work on the operator's behalf, it should
default to draining in-progress or claimed work before opening new work, even
when a scoring pass ranks an unstarted item higher. That is what a human
operator does by hand, and it is the behaviour the current tooling cannot
express.

**Evidence.** `bv`'s triage score is a weighted sum over eight components.
Urgency (weight 0.1) already rewards in-progress work — raw 1.0 for
`in_progress` against 0.8 for `open` — but it is one component among eight. A
fresh `open` task carrying a real `blocks` edge (BlockerRatio, weight 0.13) plus
a deeper unlock chain (TimeToImpact, weight 0.1) out-scores an in-progress epic
comfortably. Measured in this repo: a two-paragraph policy doc scored ~0.459
against ~0.405 for an in-progress epic covering an entire ACP client.

None of the five built-in weight presets fix this. `priority-first` raises
Urgency only to ~0.146, still not a gate, and there is no custom-weights file.
So the preference cannot be extracted from `bv` by configuration. It has to be
applied on top of its output — which is why it belongs in the engine that
consumes that output rather than in the scorer.

The sequencing policy is this issue's to define. This comment records why the
question exists and what the evidence was, so the design conversation does not
have to re-derive it.

Refs louiselm-repo-context-substrate-09r

title: Authorize unattended workflow runs with enforced capability envelopes
description:
## Problem Statement

LouiseLM can currently ask a human about ACP permission requests or auto-approve exact path and command scopes, but conversational intent, workflow authorization, harness permissions, and actual enforcement are disconnected. Tool identity is a poor proxy for consequence: a harmless tracker write may prompt while a destructive host operation may bypass LouiseLM entirely. Unattended workflow runs therefore need explicit, bounded authority whose enforcement and provenance can be demonstrated.

## Solution

Introduce run-scoped capability envelopes for policy-controlled workflow execution. The outer harness remains the hard ceiling; an operator approves the smallest proposed run envelope through a capability-diff review; every stage and worker receives only an intersected subset. LouiseLM's trusted policy layer classifies typed effects using concrete scopes and verified isolation, then allows, denies, escalates, delegates, or revokes them through trusted enforcement boundaries.

Reversibility is central but not sufficient. The model distinguishes reversible local mutation, destructive mutation, process execution, network access, data disclosure, credential use, external mutation, and cost. A sandbox changes blast radius but grants no authority: ordinary scoped repository work may use an isolated worktree, while untrusted code, unknown dependency installation, or broad unattended shell access requires launcher-attested confinement. Docker Sandboxes are one possible provider, not a product dependency or the policy source.

## User Stories

1. As an operator, I want to approve one inspectable, expiring envelope for an unattended run, so that harmless in-scope actions proceed without repeated prompts.
2. As an operator, I want high-consequence capabilities called out separately, so that “go ahead” never silently grants credentials, network access, cost, or external mutations.
3. As a workflow author, I want stages to propose narrower authority profiles without being able to authorize themselves.
4. As a coordinator, I want worker authority to attenuate through delegation, so that a child can never amplify the run's permissions.
5. As an operator, I want durable explanations for every policy decision and immediate revocation without storing secrets or pretending external effects were rolled back.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. A workflow may propose an envelope, but unattended execution starts only after explicit operator approval. The effective envelope is the intersection of outer harness ceiling, approved run envelope, current stage, exact task/worker scope, and verified isolation capabilities.
2. The run-start UI presents a human-readable capability diff plus the machine manifest. It groups local roots, process execution and isolation, network destinations, credentials, external mutations, cost ceilings, delegation depth, expiry, and human gates. Routine scoped local effects may be approved together; credentials, external mutations, costs, open network, and weakened isolation require separate opt-ins. Harness-impossible capabilities are shown unavailable.
3. Grants expire with the workflow run. Project configuration, beads fields/labels, conversational phrases, named profiles, and remembered permissions may propose or narrow policy but cannot authorize a future run or expand its envelope.
4. Stages receive declared subsets. A worker receives the explicit intersection of run, stage, parent, task, and isolation capabilities. Credentials are separate and task-required; further delegation requires an explicitly delegable capability. Worker death/completion revokes its grant.
5. LouiseLM's trusted policy layer classifies typed effects for filesystem reads/writes, destructive mutation, process execution, network, disclosure, credentials, external mutation, and cost. It combines descriptors with actual arguments, normalized scopes/destinations, and launcher-attested isolation. Agent intent and friendly tool labels cannot lower risk; missing or contradictory evidence fails closed.
6. Arbitrary commands retain unknown secondary effects unless confinement makes those effects structurally impossible. Ordinary scoped edits/tests may run in isolated worktrees; untrusted code, unknown dependency installation, or broad unattended shell access requires verified confinement. No provider-specific sandbox dependency is required.
7. Every granted effect maps to a trusted enforcement boundary: a mediating launcher/harness, LouiseLM-owned executor, or verified filesystem/network/credential confinement. Startup computes coverage; uncovered effects are removed or force interactive mode. ACP permission prompts, prompts/tool descriptions, and agent promises alone never count as enforcement.
8. An optional out-of-envelope action is denied so the agent may adapt. A required action pauses at a durable checkpoint and emits one deduplicated escalation containing the requested effect and reason, rejecting boundary, affected scopes/destinations/credential class/cost, isolation evidence, and narrowest proposed expansion. Approval adds only that capability; rejection triggers replanning or graph blocking.
9. Policy prevents equivalent operations from evading a decision through splitting or disguise. Unknown/unclassifiable actions fail closed.
10. Revocation atomically narrows authority before cleanup, cancels affected requests where possible, revokes network/credentials at their enforcement boundaries, and stops children that cannot continue. Local work is preserved for inspection rather than auto-reverted. Completed external effects are explicitly remediated and never described as rolled back. Resumption requires a fresh grant.
11. A durable run manifest records approval/time, envelopes, policy/classifier version, session/worker/bead identities, isolation profile, scopes/destinations/credential classes/cost ceilings/expiry/delegation rules, and the enforcing boundary for each capability. An append-only decision log records allow, deny, escalate, narrow, expand, delegate, and revoke outcomes with matching policy rules.
12. Authorization records contain normalized effect classes and scopes, not prompts, full commands/diffs, environments, credential values, or tool payloads. Beads receives a concise summary and local evidence reference. Local records have explicit retention/deletion rules; required audit-storage failure pauses unattended execution.
13. Existing `ask-human`, `auto-approve-scoped`, and remembered permission behavior remains safe for interactive sessions. A remembered allow cannot exceed the active envelope; a remembered deny may narrow it. Unknown ACP requests remain non-automatic.
14. Deterministic tests cover envelope intersection, stage changes, separate high-consequence opt-ins, expiry, delegation attenuation, escalation deduplication, revocation ordering, privacy-bounded logging, sandbox-attestation mismatch, missing audit storage, and an adversarial mock agent attempting undeclared filesystem, process, network, and credential effects.

## Implementation Notes

- Extend the established permission-policy boundary rather than putting authorization logic in UI, prompts, tool names, or agent configuration.
- Keep policy classification pure and separate from Neovim UI, process launch, sandbox attestation, credential injection, and durable storage.
- Treat workflow definitions as proposals: `louiselm-qbr.3` owns persisted stages; this feature owns approval, enforcement, escalation, delegation, and revocation during execution.
- Reuse the quarantine and preserved-work handoff from `louiselm-qbr.6` when revocation or policy failure stops a worker.
- Docker Sandboxes evidence informed the generic isolation profile: direct read-write mounts, clone mode, host-side MCP execution, network policy, and credential proxies must be represented as capabilities/gaps rather than collapsed into a boolean “sandboxed”.

## Testing Notes

- Use pure policy tests plus the existing mock ACP agent; no real credentials, network, Docker, or coding-agent binaries.
- Model both cooperative agents that emit ACP permission requests and non-cooperative agents that omit or bypass them.
- Exercise fast-event/process boundaries through the production scheduling path when enforcement or revocation affects Neovim state.
- Verify logs by schema and absence of sensitive fields, not by snapshots containing real payloads.

## Out of Scope

- Treating reversibility as the only consequence dimension.
- Tool-name allowlists, prompt instructions, `ready-for-agent`, or conversational phrases as grants.
- A permanent project-wide grant or opaque “yolo” mode.
- Docker Sandboxes or any other isolation provider as a mandatory runtime dependency.
- Model/worker self-classification or self-attestation.
- Ambient inheritance of all parent permissions.
- Automatic rollback of completed external effects or concurrent local work.
- Raw transcript, environment, prompt, diff, command, credential, or tool-payload archives.

title: Run isolated parallel workers and coordinate integration
description:
## Problem Statement

LouiseLM's parallel milestone needs workers to execute independent beads concurrently without fragmenting tracker truth, colliding on claims, broadening their own authority, or closing work before integration is proven. Isolated Git worktrees make code work separable, but tracker state, lifecycle recovery, blocker promotion, and final integration still need one coherent ownership model.

## Solution

Run each worker as a first-class LouiseLM-spawned ACP session in an isolated Git worktree while every worker uses one canonical shared beads database. Workers may claim, comment, file findings, and hand off work in that graph; the coordinator alone selects authorized work, promotes discoveries to blockers, integrates branches, advances integration gates, closes tasks, and commits the canonical `.beads` export.

Candidate selection is a two-stage decision: `br` supplies the authorized currently-ready set, and `bvr` ranks or assigns parallel tracks only within that set. A worker receives one exact bead and atomically claims it with its attributable session identity.

The workflow policy makes handoff and rework first-class states. A worker moves `in_progress -> ready_for_integration` only with an atomic evidence comment. That state is not ready work and cannot be closed by a worker. After integration and combined verification, the coordinator satisfies an `integration_verified` gate and closes the bead. Rejected integration moves through `rework -> in_progress`; `rework` belongs to the policy's ready group.

## User Stories

1. As an operator, I want parallel workers isolated from one another while seeing the same task graph, so that concurrency does not fork tracker truth.
2. As a coordinator, I want graph eligibility separated from graph ranking, so that a high-scoring but unauthorized or out-of-scope bead is never dispatched.
3. As a worker, I want to record findings immediately and hand off verifiable work without pretending it is integrated.
4. As a coordinator, I want to validate discoveries before they become blockers and to resume preserved partial work after a blocker clears.
5. As an operator, I want dead-worker recovery and tracker checkpoints to preserve attribution and evidence without copying sensitive raw logs by default.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Each spawned worker is an attributable ACP session with its own worktree, cwd, branch/HEAD, permissions, transcript/session identity, and atomic beads claim.
2. Worker startup resolves `br where --json` to the canonical database, relying on upstream linked-worktree discovery (beads_rust commit 44c7a6f0 / PR #429, resolving through `commondir` to the primary checkout's `.beads`), present since `br` v0.4.0. A worker never runs `br init`, and a canonical-path mismatch fails startup before work begins.
3. The coordinator computes an authorized, currently-ready candidate set with `br`, intersects it with `bvr` ranking/parallel-track output, and dispatches an exact bead. `bvr` output alone cannot authorize or claim work, and its suggested bare status command is never used.
4. Workers may inspect and file discoveries freely, but execution scope expands only for a genuine blocker. A worker records a non-blocking discovery for later review and continues within its assigned scope.
5. A worker cannot promote its own discovery to a blocker. It files the issue with `discovered-from` provenance plus a structured blocker request and stops only when necessary; the coordinator validates the request before adding or changing a `blocks` edge.
6. On promotion, the coordinator adds the blocking edge first, returns the affected task to `open`, clears its claim with a durable reason, stops the worker, and quarantines its partial worktree/session. The dependency graph—not a separate `blocked` status—suppresses readiness. Closing the blocker makes the task ready again, preferentially resuming the preserved session/worktree when safe.
7. A strict `.beads/policy.yaml` defines `open -> in_progress -> ready_for_integration -> closed` and `ready_for_integration -> rework -> in_progress`. `ready_for_integration` is excluded from `workflow.status_groups.ready`; `rework` is included. The handoff transition requires an atomic evidence comment, and closure requires a coordinator-satisfied `integration_verified` gate.
8. Only the coordinator closes a work bead, and only after integrating its branch and running combined verification. Worker handoff evidence identifies the branch/HEAD, relevant tests/checks, known risks, and any preserved artifacts.
9. Positive lifecycle evidence of a known-dead spawned worker lets the coordinator recover it immediately: preserve/quarantine its worktree and session, record a durable recovery comment, release or reassign only that worker's claim, and retain attribution. Stale/abandoned thresholds remain the fallback for external sessions lacking lifecycle evidence.
10. Automatic recovery creates a bounded quarantine manifest by reference—session ID, claim, branch/HEAD, Git status, termination reason, timestamps, and relevant paths. Copying or exporting raw logs, prompts, tool payloads, environments, or a redacted evidence bundle requires a separate explicit action.
11. Only the primary/control checkout stages and commits canonical `.beads`. Workers write the shared database and allow atomic JSONL publication but never stage or commit `.beads`. After each successful integration the coordinator records the gate/closure, flushes beads, and commits integrated code with the complete point-in-time tracker snapshot. Shutdown or budget exhaustion performs a final tracker-only checkpoint if no later integration did.
12. Concurrent integration and tracker tests prove that worker claims remain attributable, JSONL publication is coherent under writes, no worker can close directly, rework resurfaces through `br ready`, blocker promotion suppresses then restores readiness, canonical database resolution fails closed, and recovery does not mutate unrelated claims or archive sensitive content.

## Implementation Notes

- Treat the coordinator as the authority boundary, not as the only tracker writer.
- Use beads workflow policy, strict transitions, transition comments, status groups, and gates rather than application-only labels for lifecycle semantics.
- `br` is upgraded to v0.4.0 (2026-08-23), which contains commit 44c7a6f0; the explicit `.beads/redirect` compatibility fallback has been retired rather than carried permanently. Linked-worktree resolution now relies solely on upstream discovery.
- Treat `bvr` as advisory graph analysis. It may return deferred or in-progress work and may emit unsafe claim commands, so intersect by bead identity with the `br`-authorized set.
- SQLite/database locking and atomic JSONL publication provide tracker concurrency. Git commits are durability checkpoints, not the source of per-mutation attribution.
- Keep open discovery cheap, but keep code execution inside the exact dispatched scope unless the coordinator authorizes a validated blocker.

## Testing Notes

- Use deterministic fake ACP workers and temporary linked worktrees; do not require live model credentials or network access.
- Exercise worker death before claim, after claim, after edits, during handoff, and after blocker discovery.
- Cover concurrent tracker writes and a coordinator checkpoint while workers continue writing; verify the commit is coherent and later mutations remain for the next checkpoint.
- Verify policy transitions and gates through `br`, including rejected direct closure and `rework` readiness.
- Verify the upstream automatic linked-worktree path (installed `br` v0.4.0, commit 44c7a6f0) resolves a fresh linked worktree's `.beads` to the primary checkout without spawning git.

## Out of Scope

- Per-worker beads databases or semantic JSONL reconciliation.
- Coordinator-only tracker writes or append-only worker journals.
- Opaque subagents as the primary execution worker.
- Workers selecting arbitrary high-ranked work, broadening scope, promoting blockers, integrating, or closing their own tasks.
- A separate `blocked` workflow status or labels standing in for lifecycle states.
- Automatic copying, exporting, or sharing of full session/log evidence.
- Redesigning `grill-me` challenger passes or the separate LouiseLM bug-report snapshot.

title: Grill-me needed: how should LouiseLM validate workflow safety?
description:
Do not resolve this question in passing; it needs a focused design session.

## Question
How should LouiseLM validate a workflow before allowing it to run, especially when the workflow can invoke Agents that may create or trigger more work?

## Context
The attention-control-plane design is intentionally moving from informal loops toward declarative workflows with stages, transitions, triggers, resolvers, Agent execution, and human attention gates. A workflow validator should catch unsafe topology before execution rather than discovering it after Agents have started.

The motivating risks are:
- recursive or unbounded Agent spawning when a workflow triggers itself indirectly;
- cycles that continually re-enter stages or regenerate work;
- no reachable human or operator escape hatch;
- cancellation and disposal paths that do not reach every active worker;
- a workflow that is structurally valid but has no terminating path;
- a workflow whose automatic transitions bypass the intended human-attention gate.

## Threads worth pulling
- Should validation be static topology analysis, a runtime budget, or both?
- What must be proven before execution: acyclicity, bounded repetition, reachable termination, reachable human override, cancellation propagation, and ownership of spawned work?
- How should intentional loops (polling, retries, review cycles) be expressed and bounded without making ordinary workflows impossible to describe?
- Is an explicit escape transition required for every workflow, or can a global emergency stop satisfy the invariant?
- How should nested Agent-created workflows be scoped, budgeted, and prevented from recursively spawning indefinitely?
- Which failures reject a workflow, which produce warnings, and which require explicit human approval?
- How can validation itself remain side-effect free and avoid starting Agents?

## Desired outcome
A small, testable validation contract for workflow definitions, including safety invariants, bounded-loop semantics, escape-hatch requirements, and the boundary between static validation and runtime enforcement.

## Out of scope
Do not implement workflow execution, spawn Agents, or settle the contract in this issue without a dedicated grill-me session.
close_reason: Resolved by maintainer in the 2026-08-26 grill-me session. Settled: two contracts (Validation, pure/frontmatter/binary/no-override, may reject; admission, Run-scoped, stops or escalates). Bounding unit is the Generator, not the back edge -- automatic Generators declare a literal bound, human-resolved ones are bounded by the human, exhaustion must exit its loop. Generated work is bounded per Run via --actor provenance, NOT by br policy.yaml: a generative loop keeps the beads graph a DAG forever, so acyclicity is not termination. Skill-invocation permission routes to louiselm-qbr.5.1 envelopes, not a second authority mechanism. Bound exhaustion Parks (Cancellation, Sessions retained) with a declared expiry that Disposes; kill and degrade rejected. Escape hatches: synthesized per-stage non-destructive human escape (reachable unilaterally, no Agent cooperation) + destructive global stop + optional authored escapes; global stop alone insufficient because it is destructive. Cancellation propagates by ownership invariant (no stage may create a worker the Run does not own) with bounded ack escalating to Disposal; limit stated -- reaches every worker LouiseLM can address, not every process. Run state lives in capture-service (ambitious and narrow: durable Run record + expiry reaper only), because Agents are vim.system children and a Park expiry enforced in Neovim is unenforceable while the editor is closed; Runs-as-beads-issues rejected. Warm/cold Park tiers, cold gated on loadSession. Assessment (model reads prose, advisory, empty envelope, never gates, stored verdicts) added at maintainer's request alongside Validation. Vocabulary promoted: Run louiselm-kdeg, Generator louiselm-4wtn, Validation louiselm-p5h0, Assessment louiselm-x29k, Park louiselm-k1fv. Work: louiselm-qbr.3.2, louiselm-qbr.3.3, louiselm-qbr.3.4.

title: Present workflow attention on paired Android
description:
## Problem Statement

When an operator is away from Neovim, a Run can require attention but has no lightweight human surface. An Agent must not gain the ability to compose arbitrary phone notifications or obtain phone-side authority.

## Solution

The durable LouiseLM service stores normalized, typed attention items and exposes an authenticated phone inbox for the paired Android app. Neovim remains the rich cockpit. The app is a second human attention surface: it shows a decision card after the operator opens it. A later, explicit opt-in may add opaque push wakeups; notification payloads contain no transcript, prompt, path, command, issue title, or other work detail.

## User Stories

1. As an operator away from Neovim, I want to see that a Run needs attention, so I can return to the right decision.
2. As an operator, I want notification delivery to be private and bounded, so background alerts do not disclose my work.
3. As a maintainer, I want Agents to emit typed attention events rather than arbitrary notification text, so an Agent cannot spam or socially engineer the operator.

## Acceptance Criteria

1. Given a typed Run attention event, when it is recorded, then the paired Android app can fetch an authenticated human-facing attention card.
2. Given duplicate events for the same unresolved decision, when they arrive, then one attention item is presented rather than notification spam.
3. Given a phone notification, when it is delivered, then its payload contains only opaque wakeup metadata and no work detail.
4. Given an Agent-originated event, when it is malformed or not a recognized attention type, then no phone-facing notification is created.
5. Given push delivery is not configured, when attention is required, then the in-app inbox remains available and no external notification provider is contacted.

## Implementation Notes

- Keep attention state in the durable Rust service alongside Run records, but separate from capture and Run-reaper modules.
- Reuse paired-device authentication; do not expose attention over the unauthenticated health route.
- Treat FCM or another push relay as a later opt-in adapter, not a runtime requirement.

## Testing Notes

- Test typed-event validation, deduplication, authenticated retrieval, and absence of sensitive fields in the push DTO.
- Use a fake delivery adapter; no real device, credential, or network service is required.

## Out of Scope

- Remote Agent control from the phone.
- Arbitrary Agent-authored notification text.
- Push-provider setup or background delivery in the first slice.
- Replacing Neovim as the full workflow cockpit.

title: render-post fragments are not byte-identical across runs; CSS rule order varies
description:
`render-post.sh` documents its output as "a pure function of the current input"
and promises that "running twice against unchanged input is byte-identical".
It is not. Ten consecutive runs against identical input, in an identical
environment, produced four distinct fragment files. The difference is CSS rule
ordering, so the rendered page is unaffected — but the contract is false and
the test that claims to check it passes anyway.

## Observed

Found by QA case 9 of the round covering `ec19281..HEAD`, on build `daf3dfc`,
2026-08-20. Real post, real conversation excerpt (`:lines: 1481-1522`).

`blog.md` and `myst.yml` are byte-identical across runs. The fragment is not:

```
run  1  942aeb6aa0d2bbc13473e42d635ea066
run  2  b357a62c877f12da018565305d648c68
run  3  b357a62c877f12da018565305d648c68
run  4  07d64a69bd68ef675f020bcacd527080
run  5  5e4da75d9e1bbcd9942792ffa7a53d1e
...
```

Four distinct outputs across ten runs. Not environment-dependent — holding
`TERM` fixed still flips it:

```
TERM=dumb run 1  5e4da75d
TERM=dumb run 2  942aeb6a
TERM=dumb run 3  5e4da75d
```

The whole diff between two variants:

```
10d9
< .-conceal {}
12a12
> .-conceal {}
16a17
> .-markup-strong {color: #e78284; font-weight: bold}
18d18
< .-markup-strong {font-weight: bold; color: #e78284}
```

Rule order within the `<style>` block, and property order within a rule. The
`<pre>` markup is identical every time; the CSS is semantically identical every
time.

## Symptoms

- Re-rendering an unchanged post rewrites its fragment with different bytes.
- Fragments are written into the post directory and referenced from
  `myst.yml` `static_files`, so they are committed alongside a post — every
  re-render therefore dirties the working tree with a semantically null diff.
- No visual difference. The published page is correct in every variant.

## Root cause

Neovim's `:TOhtml` builds its `<style>` block by iterating the highlight groups
it collected with `pairs()`, whose order is unspecified in Lua and varies
between processes. `render-post.mjs` extracts that block verbatim
(`extractTagBlock`, then `buildFragmentDoc`), by design — `render-post.sh`'s
header states the style and `<pre>` are taken "unmodified (no selector
rewriting)".

So the non-determinism originates upstream in `tohtml.lua`, and this pipeline
faithfully preserves it. The real excerpt produces 11 rules
(`.-spell .-conceal .-nospell .-none .-markup-raw .rainbow2 .Whitespace
.Special .-tag-delimiter .-markup-strong .-tag`), which is enough for the
ordering to vary.

## Why it was not caught

`blog/scripts/test-render-post.sh` part 2 does exactly the right check —
`diff -rq "$run1_dir" "$run2_dir"` over fragments, `blog.md` and `myst.yml`.
It passes because its fixture is too small to expose the bug: the excerpts are
`:lines: 9-12` and `:lines: 16-20` of a hand-written fixture transcript that is
plain prose plus a two-line shell block and a three-line Lua snippet. That
yields a handful of highlight groups, and with few enough rules the iteration
order does not visibly change. The assertion is sound; the fixture is not
representative.

This is the same fixture-scale gap as louiselm-msg (skills discovery) and
louiselm-cmr (single-line tool titles): invented fixtures are well-behaved in
exactly the dimension the real data is not.

## Fix direction

There is a genuine conflict here, which is why this is filed rather than
patched.

Sorting the CSS is the obvious fix — normalise rule order and property order in
`render-post.mjs` before `buildFragmentDoc`. But `test-render-post.sh` part 1
asserts that the fragment's embedded `<style>`/`<pre>` match an *independent*
TOhtml capture byte-for-byte, and that capture would be unsorted. Sorting
therefore breaks part 1 unless part 1 normalises identically — at which point
"byte-for-byte against a real TOhtml capture", the property part 1 exists to
protect, is weakened to "byte-for-byte after our own normalisation".

Options, none free:

1. Sort in `render-post.mjs`, and normalise part 1's comparison the same way.
   Deterministic output; part 1 becomes a slightly weaker guarantee.
2. Sort in `tohtml-driver.lua` before the raw capture is written, so both the
   pipeline and part 1's independent capture see sorted input. Keeps part 1
   byte-exact against what the driver produces, but the driver is then no
   longer a transparent TOhtml wrapper.
3. Weaken the documented contract to semantic rather than byte equality, and
   compare parsed rule sets in part 2. Honest, but gives up the cheap
   `diff -rq` check and the "pure function of input" claim.
4. Fix upstream in Neovim's `tohtml.lua` and pin a version. Correct, slowest,
   outside this repo.

Recommend 1: it puts the normalisation where the pipeline already takes
responsibility for assembling the document, and the weakening of part 1 is
small and explicit. Whatever is chosen, `render-post.sh`'s header must stop
claiming byte-identical output until it is true.

## Acceptance

- Ten consecutive runs against unchanged input produce ten identical
  fragments.
- `test-render-post.sh` part 2's fixture is enlarged until it produces enough
  highlight groups to have caught this — otherwise the same gap remains.
- `render-post.sh`'s header contract matches the implemented behaviour.

## Not covered

- Whether `.rainbow2` and similar plugin-provided groups make the group set
  itself vary between runs (as opposed to only its order) is unverified; every
  observed variant had the same 11 rules, but that is 10 samples.
- Neovim's `tohtml.lua` has not been read to confirm `pairs()` specifically;
  the unspecified-order conclusion is inferred from the symptom.
close_reason:
Fixed by canonicalising the TOhtml <style> block inside buildFragmentDoc (blog/scripts/render-post.mjs): rules sorted by selector, declarations sorted within each rule, code-unit comparison so the output does not depend on locale. <pre> is still passed through verbatim.

Root cause verified at source rather than inferred: Neovim 0.12.2 tohtml.lua has TWO pairs() loops, line 1004 over highlight groups (rule order) and line 1032 over a group's attributes (declaration order). Sorting only rule order left 5 distinct blocks out of 10 runs; sorting both collapses to 1.

Boundary is better than the issue proposed. The issue expected part 1 of test-render-post.sh to need a matching normalisation and to be weakened by it. It does not: part 1 builds its expected fragment by calling buildFragmentDoc itself, so normalising inside that function keeps part 1 byte-exact against an independent real TOhtml capture with no change and no loss of guarantee. The filed conflict does not exist at that boundary.

All three acceptance criteria met:
- Ten consecutive runs against unchanged input are byte-identical (new part 2 check; two runs used to pass by luck).
- Part 2's fixture enlarged until it would have caught this: the excerpts now carry bold, italic, inline code, a link, a blockquote, a list and two fenced languages, producing 30 CSS rules against the old fixture's handful. Proof it is now representative: with the enlarged fixture and the fix reverted, the suite fails 4 checks (part 1, part 2 two-run, part 2 ten-run, part 2b) where it previously passed 20/20 -- the old fixture was masking this in three more places than the one it was filed against.
- render-post.sh's header contract and render-post.mjs's overview no longer claim the CSS is unmodified, and state what the canonicalisation is and why.

Independent verification outside the fixture: the 10 real TOhtml captures used to reproduce the bug (7 distinct raw style blocks) produce exactly 1 distinct fragment after buildFragmentDoc.

Gates: blog/scripts/test-render-post.sh 21 passed 0 failed; stylua --check . exit 0; lua-language-server --check . --checklevel=Warning no problems found; MiniTest full suite Fails (0) Notes (0); git diff --check clean.

Not done, deliberately: option 4 from the issue, fixing pairs() ordering upstream in Neovim's tohtml.lua. It is still the root-cause fix, but it now has no user-visible effect on this pipeline.

comments.author: lotso
comments.text:
Both 'Not covered' items resolved during the fix.

1. The group SET is stable; only ordering varies. Ten captures of a rich markdown buffer (bold, italic, inline code, link, blockquote, list, bash fence, lua fence -> 30 rules) gave 7 distinct raw style blocks, but parsing them into {selector -> sorted declarations} maps yielded exactly 1 distinct map, and 1 distinct selector set. So .rainbow2 and friends do not come and go. Sorting is therefore sufficient, not just cosmetic.

2. pairs() confirmed at source, not inferred. Neovim 0.12.2, runtime/pack/dist/opt/nvim.tohtml/lua/tohtml.lua: line 1004 'for hlid, name in pairs(state.highlights_name)' emits one rule per highlight group (rule order), and line 1032 'for attr, val in pairs(c)' emits the declarations inside a rule (property order). Two independent pairs() loops, which is why normalising rule order alone was not enough -- sorting only the style lines still left 5 distinct blocks out of 10.

Fix took option 1 but at a better boundary than the issue proposed. The issue assumed normalising in render-post.mjs *before* buildFragmentDoc, which would have forced test-render-post.sh part 1 to normalise separately and weakened it. But part 1 builds its expected fragment BY CALLING buildFragmentDoc itself, so putting normalizeStyleBlock inside buildFragmentDoc makes part 1 normalise identically for free. Part 1 keeps its exact property: 'fragment == the same builder applied to an independent real TOhtml capture'. Nothing was weakened, and the conflict that got this filed rather than patched does not exist at that boundary.

The <pre> block was verified deterministic across all 10 captures and is still passed through verbatim.
